einzeiler: Rodney Peete reflects on his football legacy, autism advocacy, and fatherhood.
kurzfassung: Former USC and NFL quarterback Rodney Peete joins the show to discuss his legendary athletic career and his transition into leadership and philanthropy. He opens up about his initial denial after his son's autism diagnosis and how shifting his perspective transformed their relationship. Peete also highlights the nearly three decades of work by the HollyRod Foundation supporting families affected by autism and Parkinson's disease.
stichpunkte: Rodney Peete reflects on growing up with supportive parents and an older brother who pushed him in competitive sports.
He discusses the mental aspects of playing quarterback and the importance of instilling belief in teammates.
Peete shares how he initially struggled with ego and denial following his son RJ's autism diagnosis.
He explains how learning to see the world through his son's eyes fundamentally changed their relationship and his approach to parenting.
The conversation covers his best-selling book and how its lessons on compassion and inclusion extend far beyond the autism community.
Peete details the nearly 30-year history of the HollyRod Foundation, which he and his wife Holly founded to support Parkinson's and autism.
He highlights a partnership with American Airlines to create sensory-friendly travel spaces and airport rooms for families with special needs.
In a rapid-fire round, Peete reveals he almost attended Stanford, names Reggie White as the toughest defensive player he faced, and shares leadership lessons from his father.

clips.hook: Always feeling like the best player
clips.text: Reflecting on his upbringing, the guest notes that he always felt like the strongest competitor both in athletic competitions and in the classroom.

clips.hook: What counts as a great game
clips.text: The conversation touches on how quarterback statistics have shifted dramatically over the decades, noting that completing seventeen passes for under three hundred yards used to be considered an exceptional performance.
During an early medical evaluation, a developmental pediatrician outlined numerous bleak milestones and limitations that parents of children on the autism spectrum were told to anticipate.
Realizing that his initial approach was entirely wrong, the guest explains how adopting his son's perspective completely transformed their relationship and made him the father he wanted to be.
When asked how he wants his memoir to be summarized, the former athlete states that his defining trait was leaving nothing on the table and maximizing every ounce of his ability.
